name: Creating a Dictionary of Character-Words Pairs
description:
Construct a program that has a function which receives a string and creates a dictionary that maps each character to the list of distinct words in the given string that start with that character. The dictionary should be case insensitive.
For example, if the given string is "This is my test score", the program creates the following dictionary:
t : ['this', 'test']
i : ['is']
m : ['my']
s : ['score']

comments.content:
We need to first declare the function that receives a string from the user and creates a dictionary that maps each character to the list of distinct words in the given string that start with that character. The given string is referred by variable s.

Note that all statements following the header line are indented.

We first need to define a dictionary referred by variable res_dict for storing the characters and distinct words in the given string that start with those characters. We initialize it with an empty dictionary by setting it to a pair of braces {}.

We need dictionary to store key-value pairs where each key represents a character and the value that is mapped to that key represents the list of words starting with that character.
We need to convert all characters in the given string to lowercase because we want a case-insensitive dictionary.

The function lower() returns a copy of the string in which all case-based characters have been lowercased. Note that to change the content of variable s, we need to set variable s to the value returned from the function lower().
We need to split the given string into words and store the words in a list.

We use split() function with no arguments because we want the split function to separate strings using space character. Note that, by default, this function considers any number of whitespace characters as a word boundary.
We want to iterate over the words in the given string and create a list of the words starting with the same character. We can use a for loop to iterate through the words in the given string.
This for loop assigns the name word to each of the values in the list of words in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each character.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

To determine if the first character of the visited word already exists as the key in the dictionary, we employ the in operator to test membership. Because the in operator implicitly scans the keys in the dictionary looking for a match.
word[0] gives us the character at index 0 of the visited word.
If the first character of the visited word already exists as the key in the dictionary, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.

When the first character of the visited word already exists as the key in the dictionary, we need to run another test for checking whether the visited word has not been added to the dictionary before. We need this additional test because we want the list of words that start with the same characters to contain distinct words.
To determine if the word does not exist in the list mapped to its first character, we could employ the not in operator.
If the word does not exist in the list mapped to its first character, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
When the word does not exist in the list mapped to its first character, we call the function append(word) to add the word to the end of that list.

When the first character of the visited word does not exist as the key in the dictionary, we need to add a new entry to the dictionary with the first character of the visited word as the key and the list with that word as its value.

The statement inside the body of this else statement is executed when the first character of the visited word does not exist as the key in the dictionary. Otherwise, the body of this else statement is skipped.
We need to add the first character of the visited word as a new key to the dictionary. We need to initialize the value mapped to this key with a list.

To see the characters and list of words starting with those characters, we need to iterate over the keys in the dictionary and print the value that is mapped to each key. We can use a for loop to iterate through the keys in the dictionary.

This for loop assigns the name char to each of the keys in the dictionary in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each character.

Note that each key in the dictionary represents a character.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

This statement prints to the default standard output stream the visited key in the dictionary, the string ":" and the value that is mapped to that key.
Each key represents a character and the value that is mapped to that represents the list of words that start with that character in the given string.
The printed text shows the arguments of the print function separated by the default delimiter (i.e., single space character) and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

We need to read the string that the user enters. To read the user input from command line, we use the input() function. This statement prints a text on the screen "Enter a string: ", then reads the text entered by the user.

The value that will be read is a string; we assign it to variable s.
This statement calls the create_dictionary function and passes the string that the user enters as its argument. Note that the function call must be done after the function is declared.
